cards.front: A blastula is a hollow early embryo surrounding a fluid-filled cavity called the {{c1::blastocoel}}.
cards.quote: The blastula is the early embryo, a hollow ball of cells around a fluid-filled cavity, the blastocoel.

cards.front: Which germ layer makes up the Xenopus animal cap and gives rise to both skin and nervous tissue?
cards.back: Ectoderm, the outer germ layer.
cards.quote: It is made of ectoderm, the outer germ layer

cards.front: In the frog embryo, the organizer lies at the {{c1::dorsal lip}} of the blastopore.
cards.quote: The organizer is the tissue at the blastopore's dorsal lip.

cards.front: In developmental biology, what does it mean for ectoderm to be competent to respond to an inducing signal?
cards.back: It is able to respond to that signal at its current developmental stage.
cards.quote: while the ectoderm is competent, able to respond, early in development.

cards.front: Why does an intact Xenopus animal cap become epidermis even when cultured without an organizer?
cards.back: The cap's own BMP signaling keeps nuclear pathway output high and promotes epidermal fate; no attached organizer is needed to supply that skin-promoting signal.
cards.quote: Cut out the cap and culture it alone in salt solution, and it becomes epidermis

cards.front: In an ectoderm culture assay, epidermal keratin marks epidermal differentiation. A treatment lowers keratin, but neural markers are not measured. Does this demonstrate neural induction?
cards.back: No. Reduced epidermal differentiation alone does not demonstrate neural identity. Measure neural gene expression as a separate readout.
cards.quote: Any treatment that makes it switch on neural genes reveals what that treatment can induce in this tissue.

cards.front: A defective protein that interferes with working copies has a {{c1::dominant-negative}} effect.
cards.quote: This is a dominant negative: a broken copy that blocks the working copies.

cards.front: How can a receptor lacking its kinase domain inhibit signaling even when normal receptors remain present?
cards.back: It still binds ligand and pairs with normal partners, but cannot transmit the signal, so complexes containing it are jammed.
cards.quote: it cannot pass the signal on, so it jams the complexes it joins.

cards.front: How does BMP receptor activation transmit a signal to the nucleus?
cards.back: BMP brings type II and type I receptors together. Type I phosphorylates Smad1, 5 or 8, which enters the nucleus with Smad4 to regulate target genes.
cards.quote: the type I receptor then phosphorylates Smad1, 5 or 8, which moves to the nucleus with Smad4 and turns on target genes

cards.front: Xenopus caps expressing the truncated activin-family receptor became neural without detectable mesoderm. Why did the absence of mesoderm matter?
cards.back: It supported neuralization by blocking receptor signaling in ectoderm, rather than through newly induced mesoderm that then induced neural tissue.
cards.quote: Neural tissue, with no mesoderm detected that could have induced it.

cards.front: A defective receptor blocks signals from several related ligands and changes a cell's fate. Can that result alone identify which ligand normally prevents the new fate? Explain.
cards.back: No. A shared blockade does not distinguish the ligands. Perturb candidate ligands individually or test which one restores the original fate.
cards.quote: It had been built from an activin receptor, but it also blocks signaling by related ligands.

cards.front: What fate do Xenopus animal-cap cells adopt after being kept separated for hours and then allowed to reaggregate?
cards.back: Neural tissue rather than epidermis.
cards.quote: Instead of epidermis, the cells made neural tissue.

cards.front: Why was adding BMP4 to separated Xenopus cap cells a useful test of its role in epidermal fate?
cards.back: Separated cells otherwise become neural. BMP4 restored epidermis and kept neural genes off, showing it could restore the skin-promoting signal in this assay.
cards.quote: Epidermis, and their neural genes stayed off. The ligand alone was enough to restore skin.

cards.front: What does neural fate being the default mean in early Xenopus animal-cap cultures?
cards.back: Competent ectoderm becomes neural when BMP pathway output is kept low, with other required inputs intact. It does not mean neural development requires no signals.
cards.quote: It names the outcome in these cultures, with the cells competent and their other inputs intact.

cards.front: A model assigns low nuclear signaling output to a culture because the culture becomes neural. Can the fate measurement also be reported as a direct measurement of nuclear output?
cards.back: No. That output is inferred from the model. A direct nuclear signaling assay is needed to test the inference independently of cell fate.
cards.quote: The fourth column is the model's reading of each row; it was not measured directly in every case.

cards.front: How does MAPK lower nuclear Smad1 output in separated Xenopus animal-cap cells?
cards.back: MAPK phosphorylates Smad1's linker region. This can keep Smad1 out of the nucleus and mark it for destruction, even while BMP receptors continue signaling.
cards.quote: MAPK phosphorylates Smad1 in its middle, or linker, region. That can keep Smad1 out of the nucleus and mark it for destruction.

cards.front: MAPK activity is selectively blocked while competent Xenopus cap cells are kept separated. Other required inputs remain intact. What happens to their usual neuralization, and why?
cards.back: Neuralization should be prevented: separated cells need MAPK activity to damp Smad1 output, while their BMP receptors continue signaling.
cards.quote: The cells need this MAPK activity to turn neural.

cards.front: Why can added BMP4 restore epidermis in separated Xenopus cap cells despite their sustained MAPK activity?
cards.back: MAPK only partially damps the pathway. Enough added BMP4 can raise nuclear pathway output sufficiently to promote epidermis.
cards.quote: the damping is partial, so enough added BMP4 can push the pathway's output back up.

cards.front: A developmental model links low nuclear output of a skin-promoting pathway to neural fate. Separated cells become neural. Design a paired measurement that distinguishes complete loss of receptor stimulation from inhibition downstream of active receptors.
cards.back: Measure receptor activity and nuclear pathway output in the same condition. Active receptors with low nuclear output favor downstream inhibition; inactive receptors with low output are compatible with loss of stimulation. This uses the rule that receptor activity and downstream output can diverge.
cards.quote: But later work found that BMP receptors keep signaling in separated cells.

cards.front: The three organizer-secreted BMP antagonists emphasized in frog neural induction are Chordin, Noggin and {{c1::Follistatin}}.
cards.back: Each binds BMP outside the cell.
cards.quote: The involuting mesoderm secretes Chordin, Noggin and Follistatin

cards.front: During frog gastrulation, the inward turning and spreading of dorsal mesoderm beneath ectoderm is called {{c1::involution}}.
cards.quote: during gastrulation, the organizer and the dorsal mesoderm turn inward and spread beneath the ectoderm. This is involution.

cards.front: Why would starting the account of frog neural induction with mesoderm involution miss an earlier contribution?
cards.back: Dorsal animal cells already produce Chordin and Noggin at the blastula stage, so neural induction starts before gastrulation.
cards.quote: Chordin and Noggin are made early, at the blastula stage, in dorsal animal cells, so neural induction starts before gastrulation.

cards.front: A researcher proposes that Noggin neuralizes Xenopus caps only by first inducing dorsal mesoderm. What marker comparison would challenge that explanation, and what result is expected?
cards.back: Assay neural and dorsal-mesoderm markers together. Noggin should induce neural markers without dorsal mesoderm, supporting a direct action on ectoderm through extracellular BMP capture.
cards.quote: Neural tissue, without dorsal mesoderm, so Noggin was acting on the ectoderm directly.

cards.front: How can Follistatin inhibit BMP signaling without preventing BMP from docking on its receptor?
cards.back: It can remain bound to BMP during receptor docking, forming a non-signaling three-part complex. Noggin and Chordin instead block receptor binding.
cards.quote: it can stay bound to BMP as BMP docks on its receptor, forming a three-part complex that does not signal.

cards.front: In a simplified culture model, total BMP4 is 1.0 nM and neural fate requires free BMP4 at or below 0.2 nM. Assume each Noggin dimer binds one BMP4 dimer completely until Noggin runs out; all concentrations count dimers. What percentage of BMP4 must be bound at the threshold, and what bound concentration does that represent?
cards.back: Bound BMP4 = 1.0 − 0.2 = 0.8 nM. Bound fraction = 0.8/1.0 = 0.80, or 80%. Under the assumed binding rule, 0.8 nM Noggin supplies this capacity.
cards.quote: it binds BMP4 and keeps it off its receptors

cards.front: After simultaneous depletion of Chordin, Noggin and Follistatin in Xenopus tropicalis, dorsal structures including the neural plate are lost. How does this extend the cap-culture evidence?
cards.back: It supports a requirement for these antagonists in normal whole-embryo neural-plate formation, beyond their ability to neuralize isolated caps. The loss fits BMP signaling remaining high.
cards.quote: The embryos lost their dorsal structures, the neural plate among them.

cards.front: Frog embryos lacking normal organizer signals form massive amounts of brain when BMP2, BMP4 and BMP7 are depleted. Which usual organizer function does this manipulation bypass?
cards.back: It bypasses the need for the organizer to lower BMP signaling through secreted antagonists. It does not establish independence from other required inputs such as early FGF signaling.
cards.quote: The embryos formed massive amounts of brain, even without normal organizer signals.

cards.front: Why is early FGF signaling more than an optional way to inhibit BMP during frog neural induction?
cards.back: Early FGF signaling is also required in caps and embryos. It can lower Smad output through MAPK, but also has functions that BMP inhibition does not explain.
cards.quote: Early FGF signaling is also needed for neural induction, in the embryo and in caps, in addition to BMP inhibition

cards.front: Which frog signaling proteins correspond to the fly proteins Dpp and Sog?
cards.back: Dpp is a BMP2/4 relative; Sog is a Chordin relative.
cards.quote: Its gene decapentaplegic (dpp) encodes a BMP2/4 relative, and short gastrulation (sog) encodes a relative of Chordin.
cards.section: The same contest in a fly, upside down

cards.front: How do the dorsal–ventral maps of BMP-family signals, antagonists and neural tissue compare in fly and vertebrate embryos?
cards.back: Fly: Dpp dorsal, Sog ventrolateral, nerve cord ventral. Vertebrate: BMP4 signaling high ventrally, Chordin from dorsal organizer, neural tube dorsal. Neural tissue forms on the low-BMP side.
cards.quote: In both animals, nervous system forms where the antagonist keeps the BMP signal low.
cards.section: The same contest in a fly, upside down

cards.front: Frog Chordin works in the fly and fly Sog works in the frog. What does this cross-species swap show beyond similarity of their expression patterns?
cards.back: It supports conserved antagonist function: each can act in the other species' signaling system. This is functional evidence beyond a matching spatial arrangement.
cards.quote: frog Chordin works in the fly and fly Sog works in the frog.
cards.section: The same contest in a fly, upside down

cards.front: How do activation and transformation separate neural induction from head-to-tail patterning in Nieuwkoop's framework?
cards.back: Activation produces neural tissue with anterior character. Transformation shifts some of it toward hindbrain and spinal cord; BMP antagonists resemble activators rather than posteriorizing signals.
cards.quote: activation, which makes ectoderm neural and anterior, and transformation, which shifts part of it toward hindbrain and spinal cord.

cards.front: A treatment induces a general neural marker in ectoderm. A researcher concludes that it has produced spinal cord. What additional evidence is needed, and why does neural induction alone not settle that conclusion?
cards.back: Test head-to-tail regional identity with appropriate regional markers. The governing rule separates neural identity from positional identity: neural induction does not establish posterior character, and an activation step can yield anterior neural tissue.
cards.quote: activation, which makes ectoderm neural and anterior, and transformation, which shifts part of it toward hindbrain and spinal cord.

cards.front: In chick epiblast, Chordin maintains early neural markers in previously induced cells but fails to initiate them outside the future neural plate. Which claim is supported: maintenance of an existing response, sufficiency for initiating neural fate, or both?
cards.back: Maintenance is supported; sufficiency for initiation in that region is not. BMP inhibition can stabilize an induced state without initiating it there.
cards.quote: Chordin did not induce early neural markers there, although it did stabilize early neural markers in cells that had already received neural-inducing signals.

cards.front: Mouse embryos lacking Chordin and Noggin still form neural tissue but have severe forebrain defects. Why does this result neither establish a universal need for these two antagonists in neural induction nor invalidate the Xenopus cap model?
cards.back: Neural tissue persists, so the result supports a forebrain requirement rather than an absolute requirement for all neural tissue. The governing rule is tissue-specific: the default model describes competent Xenopus cap ectoderm with other required inputs intact.
cards.quote: That shows the two antagonists are needed for the forebrain, not that they are needed for neural tissue as such.

cards.front: A model predicts that competent early frog cap ectoderm becomes neural when BMP signaling is blocked, provided other required inputs remain intact. Design a result that would falsify this conditional claim and name the checks needed to interpret it.
cards.back: Show epidermal keratin or failure of neural markers despite independently verified BMP blockade, preserved competence and timing, and intact required inputs including FGF. The rule is conditional; losing competence or FGF would not contradict it.
cards.quote: while its competence, timing and other required inputs such as FGF are preserved.

cards.front: In competent early Xenopus animal caps with other required inputs intact, a mutant BMP type I receptor keeps nuclear pathway output high without ligand. Compare extracellular BMP capture with complete blockade of BMP receptor kinase signaling, including the mutant: what fates do you predict, and why?
cards.back: Extracellular capture should leave epidermal fate; complete BMP receptor kinase blockade should permit neural fate. Ligand-independent activity bypasses capture, but blocking all BMP receptor kinase signaling interrupts both mutant and normal receptor activity.
cards.quote: the pathway is jammed, so BMP in the fluid has little effect.

cards.front: In the frog BMP-shuttling model, Chordin still binds and transports BMP, but Chordin cleavage is prevented. What happens to release of active BMP toward the ventral side, and why?
cards.back: Ventral BMP release should decrease because BMP remains trapped in the receptor-inaccessible Chordin complex instead of being freed by cleavage.
cards.quote: While bound to Chordin, BMP cannot reach its receptors, so it is silent as it travels.
cards.section: The shuttling mechanism, step by step

cards.front: In an illustrative free-diffusion model with no BMP removal, concentration inside a spherical cap relative to an isolated cell scales as (R/a)². For R = 200 µm and cell radii a = 25 µm and 15 µm, calculate the two ratios. Why should these not be treated as measured frog-cap values?
cards.back: For a = 25 µm: (200/25)² = 64-fold. For a = 15 µm: (200/15)² ≈ 177.8-fold, consistent with about 60–180-fold. These are illustrative spherical-model estimates; a real cap is a sheet a few cells thick, so the dilution effect would be smaller.
cards.quote: the concentration a cell inside the ball sees is roughly (R/a)² times what an isolated cell sees
cards.section: Why dilution was a good guess, and what would make it fail

cards.front: An illustrative BMP-removal model has decay length √(D/k), average lifetime 1/k, D near 2 µm²/s, and lifetimes of 5–30 minutes. Calculate the endpoint decay lengths. Does the large dilution prediction from a model with no removal necessarily survive cell separation?
cards.back: Lifetimes are 300–1800 s; lengths are √(2 × 300) ≈ 24.5 µm and √(2 × 1800) = 60 µm, about 25–60 µm. No: the removal rule favors signaling from a cell and its near neighbors, reducing dispersal's effect. This is a possible physical explanation, not a measured mechanism for frog BMP4.
cards.quote: With D near 2 µm²/s and an average lifetime of 5 to 30 minutes, the decay length is about 25 to 60 micrometres
cards.section: Why dilution was a good guess, and what would make it fail
